en: Record of the Orthodox Lineage of the Transmission of the Dharma, Scroll One, Compiled by the Śramaṇa Qiesong of Mount Dongshan in Tengzhou during the Song Dynasty.
Memorial to the Primordial Patriarch Śākyamuni Tathāgata. Memorial to the Primordial Patriarch Śākyamuni Tathāgata.
Heaven and earth begin anew,
and on Jambudvīpa there arises a king called a Mahāpuruṣa (Great Man).
When this Great Man passes away, [the world enters a new cycle].
Thereafter, successive kings followed this precedent and continued their work without ceasing;
throughout antiquity and the present, they are likely beyond counting.
Nevertheless, among them were those who were sagely and divine, possessing extraordinary virtues.
One who possesses such [virtue] is called a Wheel-Turning King (cakravartin);
one whose virtue does not reach that level is called a Minor King (kṣudraka-rāja).
Since there are degrees of greatness and smallness in virtue,
the extent of the realm they govern likewise diminishes accordingly,
decreasing from the four continents down to three, two, and so forth.
As for those who rule over all under heaven,
and those who rule over the various states—
those whom we call "Kings."
Although ten thousand billion generations may pass,
the Śākya clan shall continue its lineage without interruption;
furthermore, in a future age there will be a sovereign named Mahāsudarśana.
Mahāsammata gave birth to Uposatha;
Uposatha gave birth to Mandhātṛ; Mandhātṛ gave birth to Cara;
Cara gave birth to Upacara.
From Gaura was born Nipuṇa;
from Nipuṇa was born Siṃhahanu;
from Siṃhahanu was born Śuddhodana, also called Suddhodana; all seven of these generations were kings.
The master Māndhātṛ alone was titled a "Noble King" (Cakravartin) by Śuddhodana;
it was from this Noble King Śuddhodana that the Tathāgata emerged.
He was born in the kingdom of Madhyadeśa.
Śākya is his clan name;
Muni is a title of honor.
Long ago, the Tathāgata encountered Dīpaṃkara Buddha in a previous life.
In the great city of Padma,
he spread his hair as a mat for [the Buddha] to tread upon,
and offered a lamp with the utmost reverence.
He then received a prediction, saying:
"In the future, you shall become a Buddha just like me;
your name shall be Śākyamuni."
Throughout subsequent incalculable kalpas,
all these sages accumulated and cultivated supreme virtues until the time of Kāśyapa Buddha.
Thereupon, having attained the Way as a Bodhisattva,
he was reborn above in the Tuṣita Heaven,
assuming his position as the one destined to succeed him.
He was titled the Great Being Vimalaprabha;
he preached the Dharma in the heavens to deliver the celestial hosts.
When the time for his manifestation had duly arrived,
he assembled devas and humans to deliberate upon the place of his descent into birth.
As the assembly had not yet reached a decision,
the Great Being himself declared that the Kingdom of Kapilavastu was situated in the center of Jambudvīpa,
and that King Śuddhodana was his father.
His family has been of imperial lineage for generations;
as the ultimate manifestation of sagely virtue and a member of the Cakravartin clan,
it is fitting that he should be born through such means.
When he manifested the signs of decline for the gods,
intending to descend to transform those below,
the celestial hosts all wept.
"I pray that you will remain here longer.
The Mahāsattva then explained for him the meaning of his past lives and his intention to attain Buddhahood,
thereby releasing her from her attachments.
The Great Being immediately relinquished his celestial lifespan and manifested the descent of his spirit into the right flank of his mother,
Queen Māyā of the Śākya clan, riding upon a white elephant from the midst of the sun.
That evening, he hastily informed the king, saying,
"Please allow me to purify my person so that I may request to observe the Eightfold Precepts (Aṣṭāṅga-śīla).
The king complied with his request.
Upon seeking his dream, the Great Being entered its right side by means of his vehicle and remained there; the devas, filled with longing, became his retinue.
Simultaneously, those born among human beings were infinite in number.
From the moment of conception,
the mother’s body attains great tranquility,
and she naturally experiences the bliss of dhyāna.
As she was about to give birth,
Māyā intended to go to the park;
accordingly, the palace attendants immediately prepared a precious palanquin.
The king again issued a broad command for his attendants to follow him.
Upon reaching the foot of an *aśoka* tree in the garden,
its flowers were in full and exquisite bloom.
Later, when she wished to take him, she raised her hand;
then the Holy Son was born from her right side,
and divine dragons immediately poured down water to wash him.
The earth produced golden lotuses to support him.
Thereupon, the Holy Son took seven steps in each of the four directions and pointed up and down with his hands, saying:
"In the four intermediate directions, above, and below, I alone am most honored.
It was as if an inner attendant had joyfully entered the palace to announce this;
when the King heard it, he sent countless noble attendants along with him to go and see for himself.
He could not contain his great joy.
At that time, the celestial deities and terrestrial spirits all beheld him and offered this benediction:
"May the Great Being swiftly attain perfect enlightenment."
The king soon took it and went with him to visit the celestial temple;
the image of the deity rose up and received his prostrations.
Upon returning to the palace, he convened a great assembly of the wise.
To give him a name,
the assembly conferred upon him the title Sarvārthasiddha; subsequently,
they sought out physiognomists.
Then the seer Asita, having been summoned,
finally beheld the Holy Son;
he immediately prostrated at his feet and wept, saying:
He is the supreme sovereign of these three realms.
At the age of nineteen, he shall become a wheel-turning monarch;
otherwise, he will leave the household life and attain Buddhahood.
He delivers immeasurable numbers of people.
It is my regret that I am old and cannot witness this.
The king, concerned by the words of the seer,
guarded the child with even greater care.
When he had grown somewhat older, the king appointed a teacher to instruct him in the worldly scriptures.
The Noble Son then questioned him regarding those teachings,
but the Master was unable to provide any answer.
This extended to all the arts existing in the world, including astronomy, geography, archery, charioteering, and the various crafts.
All were able to accomplish these tasks without waiting for instruction.
Before long, he was established as the Crown Prince,
and the national treasures were entrusted to him.
However, the Sages have already attained great purity;
although they manifest marriage in accordance with the world,
they do not possess any ordinary intent.
Due to the conditions of past karma, he pointed to his consort’s belly and said,
"Six years from now, you shall give birth to a son.
One day, he prepared his carriage and desired to go on a journey.
Although he emerged through all four gates,
he encountered various things; yet in the end,
it was the sight of an old man, a sick man, a dead man, and a śramaṇa that moved him.
His resolve to renounce the world grew even more steadfast.
Upon his return, he presented his intention to his father, the King;
however, the King [opposed it], noting that the kingdom lacked a noble heir.
He then took the Prince’s hand and wept,
wishing to deter his resolve; at that moment,
a deva from the Śuddhāvāsa heaven arrived from above.
He prostrated at the Crown Prince’s feet and said,
“Great Being, you have long been devoted to supreme virtue;
now is the time for you to leave the household life.”
"You should go there.
The Prince said, "If it is as you say,"
However, the guard was extremely strict;
where could he go?
The deva then used his supernormal powers to subdue the sentries.
All were fast asleep and unable to wake.
The Prince then secretly commanded his charioteer, Chandaka;
Chandaka took the divine steed Kanthaka by the reins and brought him forward.
However, the horse was sorrowful and the charioteer wept;
the Prince comforted them.
At the break of dawn, they hurriedly departed.
The light illuminated the great trichiliocosm.
The Prince said,
"The renunciations of all Buddhas of the past were likewise thus."
Thereupon, the devas supported the hooves of the horse and received Chandaka,
[carrying them] out through the northern gate of the city.
He ascended loftily into the void and departed.
The Prince spoke again, saying:
"If one does not sever the eight sufferings, the Wheel of Dharma cannot be turned."
"If I do not attain unsurpassed bodhi, I shall never return.
The assembly of devas praised this as virtuous and recorded it for him as a vow.
Upon reaching the mountain named Candra,
he first rested briefly within the woods and then cast off his robes and cap.
He took the precious sword he wore at his waist and cut off their hair and beards,
vowing: "May I, together with all beings, sever these afflictions."
He then bestowed his hair upon Śakra,
Lord of the Devas. At that time,
a deva from the Śuddhāvāsa heaven manifested as a person and offered him a coarse cloth *saṃghāṭī*— according to another version, it was made of *mṛga-paṭṭa* (deer-cloth).
He requested that the Prince’s precious robes be exchanged for them,
thereby obtaining the dharma-robes;
wearing them, he made further progress.
The most excellent place on that mountain was called Mount Mithila-ratna.
There, in the Ālana monastery, lived an ancient hermit who,
upon seeing the Prince, paid his respects and yielded precedence to him.
He sat and discussed the Dharma with him;
then, after sending Canda back,
the father king missed him deeply.
He was determined to bring them back;
although his remonstrators would not listen,
he ultimately issued an edict to welcome them.
His ministers and subordinates came to entreat him by the tens of thousands;
yet, despite their most earnest exhortations,
he remained firm and would not turn his mind back.
He then left behind the five men, including Kauṇḍinya,
to serve as his attendants; there,
the Sage practiced the concentration of the sphere of nothingness for three years.
Subsequently, because he considered those teachings not to be ultimate, he abandoned them.

He then proceeded to the abode of Udraka Rāmaputra and practiced the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception for three years— namely, at the place where the two seers, Ārāḍa Kālāma and Udraka Rāmaputra, resided— but again found those teachings not to be ultimate.
He proceeded to Mount Gajaśīrṣa and practiced asceticism among the various non-Buddhist sectarians,
consuming only hemp and wheat daily.
After six years had passed, the non-Buddhists were also converted.
The Sage then reflected to himself, saying:
"This asceticism is not the true liberation."
"I shall receive food and thereafter attain Buddhahood.
He then bathed in the Nairañjanā River,
and the heavens caused the trees to lean over for him.
The Sage assisted him and brought him out;
he accepted the milk-gruel offered by the daughter of the cowherd and immediately proceeded to the foot of the Pippala tree.
The Lord of Devas transformed himself into a man,
who gathered auspicious grass to serve as a seat for him;
radiant clouds and propitious winds arrived together in profusion.
The celestial Māra was struck with alarm;
leading his hosts, he came to create obstacles.
The Sage pressed the earth with his finger.
The earth shook violently,
and all the Māras were cast prostrate;
thus he subdued them, and it was on the evening of the seventh day of the second month.
He entered right samādhi,
and on the eighth day at the time of the rising of the morning star,
he manifested complete and great enlightenment.
He then attained Equal and Perfect Enlightenment.
At that time, the great earth shook violently,
and auspicious signs from heaven and earth emerged in response.
Devas, māras, humans, and divine beings gathered together to pay their respects as he ascended the Vajrāsana.
The Lord of Devas served as his teacher and requested him to turn the Wheel of Dharma;
this was first for the five, including Kauṇḍinya.
Attended by his retinue while in the mountains,
he first conferred ordination upon Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana;
subsequently, he entered the Deer Park and preached the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths.
Nevertheless, those who attained the fruits of the Path because of this were also counted in the hundreds of millions.
Thereupon, he said to the bhikṣus,
"You all may become fields of merit for the world."
It was fitting that they each go forth to transform sentient beings;
the Tathāgata, however, proceeded alone to the kingdom of Magadha.
That country already possessed extraordinary individuals.
They were known as the Kāśyapa of Uruvilvā;
the three brothers had all attained the arts of the rishis.
He was quite conceited on account of his own path and had several thousand followers.
When the Tathāgata arrived, [he encountered them].
Thereupon, they all humbly followed his transformation,
and together with their followers, they all attained realization of the Way.
Previously, King Bimbisāra had possessed a Bamboo Grove Park.
It was renowned as a place of great beauty.
The king once thought to himself, "If the Tathāgata were to come to me first,
I would abandon this [place]."
The Tathāgata immediately understood his intention and proceeded to reside in that garden.
Upon hearing this, the king was overjoyed and quickly arranged a grand procession of attendants.
Not merely ten million came rushing forward.
When the Tathāgata saw them,
some among the assembly were filled with doubt.
The Tathāgata then summoned Kāśyapa and preached the Dharma for him,
in order to resolve his delusions.
The king’s retinue and immeasurable devas and humans subsequently attained the Dharma-eye;
they then offered their garden as a vihāra and invited the Tathāgata to reside there.
Not long after he had settled there,
it happened that a bhikṣu was begging for alms in Rājagṛha,
and Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana heard the Dharma from him.
Thereupon, he attained awakening.
He then returned with them, and the Tathāgata said, "Those two who have come shall become my foremost disciples. Thus it was.
He delivered him.
Previously, Mahākāśyapa had shaved off his beard and hair and entered the mountains to practice dhyāna.
One day, a deity appeared in the air and addressed him, saying:
Now that the Buddha has appeared in the world,
you have surpassed your teacher. For this reason,
as he was proceeding toward the Bamboo Grove Monastery, upon his arrival, the Tathāgata rose to greet him and, looking back at the assembly, said:
That after my parinirvāṇa the Dharma will spread and emerge for sixty thousand years is due to the power of this person.
At that time, six years had already passed since the Tathāgata attained the Way.
Yet he had never met his father, the king, even once;
the king missed him greatly.
His attendant, Udāyin, [was aware of this].
"Please go and convey to the King our feelings regarding our long separation,
and request that he allow us to return to our own country.
Once Dāyī had arrived, [he delivered this message].
The Tathāgata comforted him,
and he soon attained the Path and realized the fourth fruit.
He was then sent back to his kingdom and told his father, the King:
The Buddha returned seven days later.
When the appointed time arrived, the king traveled forty li from his capital and prepared a grand ceremonial procession to welcome the Tathāgata.
The auspiciousness moved both heaven and earth.
King Xiang was greatly delighted upon seeing him,
and consequently issued an edict for five hundred noble youths of his clan to follow him and leave the household life.
When he returned to the palace, Rāhula paid homage to him;
holding the Sage’s robe, he addressed him, saying,
"This is truly like the Tathāgata."
By means of this, she acted as a mother to resolve the multitude of their doubts;
thus her blessings were infinite,
and all living beings relied upon her.
The family and the state subsequently flourished,
and they turned toward his transformative teachings;
from that time on, he preached the Dharma according to the capacities of his listeners.
Whether in the heavens, among humans,
in the palaces of the nāgas, or in other realms,
wherever one goes, one brings about great benefit.
However, the deeds performed by his sagely spirit cannot be fully recorded; subsequently,
as the time for his transformation approached, he departed.
He then addressed Mahākāśyapa, saying:
"I now entrust to you the pure Dharma-eye, the wondrous mind of Nirvāṇa, and the subtle, sublime, and correct Dharma of the true mark that is signless."
"You should uphold and protect this,
and you must also command Ānanda as your deputy to propagate and transform others so that it shall never be interrupted.
Then he spoke in verse:
"The Dharma is fundamentally without Dharma; that which is without Dharma is also Dharma.
Now, at this time when I transmit the absence of Dharma, how has any dharma ever been a dharma?
Having spoken these verses, he further addressed Mahākāśyapa, saying:
"I shall also entrust to you this saṃghāṭī robe, sewn with golden thread.
You must transmit it to Maitreya Buddha— the Buddha of the Successive Stage— also known as Mili, awaiting his appearance in the world."
"You should guard this carefully.
Upon hearing these instructions, Mahākāśyapa prostrated at [the Buddha's] feet and praised them as excellent.
Respectfully obeying the Buddha’s command,
he went one day to the space between the twin śāla trees at Kuśinagara and addressed the great assembly.
Desiring to enter parinirvāṇa,
the Elder Cunda earnestly presented offerings; because of this,
the Tathāgata further expounded the Dharma extensively.
Thereafter, having delivered Subhadra,
he emerged from his seat through a succession of samādhis;
he drew back his saṃghāṭī robe to reveal his body, which was radiant with purple-gold light.
He entrusted his final instructions to the great assembly,
then lay down on his right side and entered a state of profound, motionless stillness.
At that time, the fourfold assembly numbered in the hundreds of millions;
gods and humans wailed in grief and yearned for him with such intensity that the entire trichiliocosm was shaken,
as celestial flowers fell like a great rain.
The ground there quaked everywhere;
when the golden coffin was brought inside,
it waited for Mahākāśyapa.
Yet the worldly fire could not ignite it.
Just as Kāśyapa arrived,
his feet emerged from both sides of the coffin.
He consoled them for their grief and longing.
Shortly thereafter, the golden coffin rose of its own accord and circumambulated the city of Pāṭaliputra;
it then descended and was cremated by the fire of samādhi, which spontaneously consumed it until nothing remained but ashes.
The radiance of Śāriputra’s relics illuminated heaven and earth;
those present at the assembly— whether gods,
humans, spirits, or nāgas— [were all moved].
They all divided and took portions of the stupa.
Consider this:
the Tathāgata’s birth occurred on the eighth day of the fourth month in the ninth year of King Zhao of the Zhou dynasty, the year of Jiayin.
His renunciation occurred on the eighth day of the second month of the twenty-seventh year of King Zhao, the year of Renshen.
His attainment of enlightenment occurred in the year of Wuyin, the thirty-third year of King Zhao.
His parinirvāṇa occurred on the fifteenth day of the second month in the thirty-sixth year of King Mu, the *renshen* year.
From his passing until now, one thousand and seventeen years have elapsed.
In the tenth year of the Yongping era of Emperor Xiaoming of the Han dynasty, the year of Dingmao, the teaching spread throughout the Middle Kingdom.
Alas! The Tathāgata manifested a lifespan equal to that of the world.
He lived for a total of seventy-nine years,
sustaining the world through the True Dharma for forty-nine years; so it is stated in the old records.
The World-Honored One left home at nineteen.
He practiced austerities in the Snowy Mountains for six years and attained enlightenment at thirty.
He dwelt in the world preaching the Dharma for forty-nine years and entered parinirvāṇa at the age of seventy-nine.
Now, calculating by means of the current year count:
If he had practiced for only six years,
his attainment of the Way would have occurred at the age of twenty-five;
yet it is said to have been at thirty.

Thus, it was necessary to spend six years in total studying the Dharma under the two sages before one could fulfill the original number [of years] to transform and deliver sentient beings, who are beyond counting.
This is the Dharma that has been taught.
The Sūtras, the Vinayas,
and the Śāstras are as vast as hundreds of thousands of great oceans;
those who explore them may attain both the shallow and the deep according to their own capacity.
Yet, when tracing it back to the distant past,
it reaches the very beginning and end of heaven and earth;
when pointing to what is near at hand, [it extends to the present].
Thus, it exhausts the formation and decay of hair and skin;
in its profundity, it reaches the ultimate limits of ghosts and spirits;
in its subtlety, it penetrates the mysteries of transformation and change.
The great necessarily encompasses both gods and humans;
the small leaves not even the insects behind.
This is the source of all calamity and fortune in the world.
The very foundation of nature and destiny is fully contained herein.
Such is the ultimate greatness of this Way.
As for the vast reach of its teachings, I regard myself as lowly and ordinary, lacking the capacity to know them; thus, I dare not praise them.
Yet I reflect that since the beginning of sentient existence, there has never been anyone more venerable than the Sage.
Since there have been sages, none has yet attained the state of a Tathāgata.
Formerly, Lie Yukou said that Confucius once told Grand Chancellor Shang:
In the West there was a sage who governed without ruling and yet remained free from disorder;
he spoke not and yet was trusted by all.
He transformed others without acting himself;
vast and boundless, the people could find no name for him.
I suspect he was a sage.
"I do not know whether he is truly a sage or truly not a sage.
The Grand Chancellor remained silent, reflecting inwardly:
"Is Kong Qiu deceiving me?"
Judging by this evidence,
the words of the Master of Lie are not spurious.
Whether the birth and parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata,
as well as his renunciation and attainment of the Way,
occurred during the reigns of Kings Zhou Zhao or King Mu;
However, from King Wu of the Zhou dynasty down to King Li,
there were no recorded years;
it was only with King Xuan that such records first appeared.
The old records state:
the ninth year, the twenty-seventh year, and the thirty-third year of King Zhao.
Regarding King Mu’s thirty-sixth year,
some have not entirely accepted this view;
I have previously examined and clarified it.
Therefore, I examined the "Genealogical Tables of the Three Dynasties" by Grand Historian Sima Qian.
Looking at its preface, it says:
"In reading the records and chronicles, I find that from the Yellow Emperor onwards, all have their years and numbers recorded."
Examining their calendrical systems, genealogies, and historical records from beginning to end,
one finds that the traditions concerning the transmission of the five elemental virtues differ across ancient texts;
these discrepancies are indeed not without reason, for how could it be mere coincidence that the Master did not arrange and sequence them according to their chronological order?
Based on this evidence,
it is clear that prior to the Three Dynasties, it was not truly the case that there were no recorded years.
Rather, because Sima Qian followed the intent of the *Shangshu* (Book of Documents) as transmitted by Confucius, he did not record the years for that period.
Thus he produced a work that stands beyond the mundane world;
where there was doubt, he recorded it as doubtful,
so that future scholars of virtue might examine it.
If figures such as Huangfu Mi had further refined and corrected it,
it would have become the established traditional genealogy of the Śākya clan.
This is corroborated by written records, which can provide detailed evidence; who would say otherwise?
The critique states:
Regarding the entrustment of the Dharma to Mahākāśyapa:
at what time did it occur, and by what means must it be made clear? It is said:
Formerly, at the beginning of the Nirvāṇa assembly,
the Tathāgata addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"You should not speak such words."
All the unsurpassed true Dharma that I now possess has been entirely entrusted to Mahākāśyapa.
As for this Kāśyapa:
"I shall serve as a great refuge for you;
this is clearly evident. This refers to the second fascicle of the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*.
As for its orthodox essence, it was indeed transmitted secretly by the sages.
One cannot fail to know its location and its timing;
when measured against the sūtras,
the Lotus Sūtra comes first.
It was only after his parinirvāṇa that he preached the Lotus Sūtra, at which Mahākāśyapa was present;
yet when [the Buddha] entered nirvāṇa, he was not among those in the assembly.
I maintain that the time of the transmission of the Dharma must lie between these two scriptures. Others,
however, say:
At the assembly on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa, the Tathāgata held up a flower to show it to them;
Kāśyapa then smiled,
and the Dharma was thereby entrusted to him.
It is further said:
The Tathāgata entrusted the Dharma to Mahākāśyapa before the Many-Sons Stūpa.
Yet the world universally regards this as the actual substance of the transmitted teachings;
however, I have never seen from where it originated,
though I have taken some small measure of it.
Nor did I dare presume this to be definitive.
It is said that at the beginning of other texts,
the seven Buddhas must invariably be enumerated.
Yet this [verse] is absent here.
Could it be that the verses of the Seven Buddhas were not translated by the ancients?
I say: not so.
Now, one who maintains the true lineage must necessarily take personal transmission from a master as its proof.
Therefore, since the time of Śākyamuni Tathāgata’s descent [into the world], I have not listed them again;
this is my own examination.
The various biographies of the *Bao-lin-zhuan* and the *Deng-ting-zhuan* all trace their lineage back to Zhi Qianglianglou of the Former Wei and Nalanda Yasas of the Eastern Wei.
These two were translated by the Brahman monks [Dharmarakṣa and Dharmagupta].
Furthermore, those that list the verses of the Seven Buddhas at the beginning likewise originated from the two translations by Zhi Qiang and Yashas.
How could it be said that this is not its original version?
However, the *Baolin zhuan* does not list the Seven Buddhas at its beginning;
this is precisely in accordance with the intent of our own text.
The Record of the Orthodox Lineage of the Transmission of the Dharma, Scroll One, concludes.

The Biography of the First Patriarch of India, Venerable Mahākāśyapa.

The Indian Second Patriarch, Venerable Ānanda, transmitted it to the Indian Third Patriarch, Venerable Śaṇavāsa; the Indian Fourth Patriarch, Venerable Upagupta, transmitted it to the Indian Fifth Patriarch, Venerable Dīdaka; the Indian Sixth Patriarch, Venerable Miśraka, transmitted it to the Indian Seventh Patriarch, Venerable Vasumitra; the Indian Eighth Patriarch, Venerable Buddhanandi, transmitted it to the Indian Ninth Patriarch, Venerable Buddhamitra; the Indian Tenth Patriarch, Venerable Pārśva, transmitted it to the Indian Eleventh Patriarch, Venerable Punayaśas; the Indian First Patriarch, Venerable Mahākāśyapa, transmitted it to Venerable Mahākāśyapa.
He was a native of the kingdom of Magadha,
of the Brahmin caste;
his father’s name was Yinze (Pīyūṣa).
His mother was named Xiangzhi.
From the moment of his birth, his physical appearance was exceptionally beautiful and flourishing;
his body was the color of gold.
Yet its radiance shone forth over a vast distance.
An interpreter said,
"This child’s past virtue is pure and eminent."
The Dharma dictates that he must leave the household life.
His parents were distressed by this and consulted one another, saying:
"One must certainly find a beautiful woman to bind her heart.
As she grows older, it is difficult to choose a husband for her;
yet the Honored One declines."
Having no other choice, he then deceived her, saying,
"I cannot take you as my consort unless your golden complexion is exactly like mine."
The parents then followed the Brahmin’s plan to cast a golden image and transport it throughout their kingdom,
seeking alms from those who came to view it.
When she eventually obtained a golden-hued woman like Kāśyapa,
he took her as his wife.
This occurred prior to the parinirvāṇa of Vipaśyin Buddha.
The multitude erected a stūpa for his relics;
the image on the face of the stūpa was golden,
yet it was damaged and broken.
At that time, Kāśyapa was serving as a goldsmith.
There happened to be a poor woman who carried a single gold coin.
Seeking to govern, he served as a scribe;
wishing to go and fill that post,

2. A Brief Transmission of the Lineage of the Main Body of the Text.
Part Two: The Eighth Generation from Dajian [Huineng] was Chan Master Wenyuan of Mount Yunmen in Shaoyou Prefecture.
He was a native of Jiaxing in Suzhou.
His surname was Zhang,
and by nature he was exceptionally intelligent and quick-witted.
In his youth, he was unlike ordinary children.
He left the household life and received the precepts.
Having studied the Sūtras, Vinaya, and Śāstras for but a short time, he mastered them all.
Furthermore, upon visiting spiritual friends,
he encountered the venerable elder Chen of Muzhou once; at that single meeting,
he attained great realization of the fundamental principle.
He subsequently sought certification from Chan Master Xuefeng Cunen;
from then on, he concealed his brilliance and mingled with the multitude.
Later, he traveled south and arrived at the Dharma assembly of Chan Master Shaoyang Lingshu Min.
Min was an extraordinary man,
renowned for his ability to perceive things with prescient insight.
Upon meeting Yan, he held him in exceptional esteem and regarded him as a vessel of great potential.
He was subsequently appointed as the first seat among the assembly.
Upon his passing, he left a letter recommending [his successor] to Liu, the ruler of Guangzhou,
who commanded that the Chan Master should succeed him in presiding over that monastery.
Subsequently, the Liu family restored the Yunmen Great Monastery and invited Xuanjian to reside there;
his fame consequently spread far and wide.
Scholars from the four quarters flocked to him like water flowing downward;
yet his moral influence was sharp and swift,
leading them ever closer to the Way.
In the world today, those who honor him and style themselves as belonging to the Yunmen School number eighty-eight dharma heirs in total.

He had long possessed far-reaching ambition;

In the evening, he again set out on his travels.

he and his companions gradually came to rest at Jizō-in Temple to the west of that province.
Having met with Chan Master Xuanzhen,
he attained the essential points of the Dharma;
he then remained in a hermitage at Gan-tai-zhou (Sugarcane Island) in Fuzhou.
Later, he again led his companions on a tour through the regions south of the Yangtze River until they reached Linchuan.
Thereupon, at the request of the local governor, he resided at Chongshou Monastery.
From that time on, his circle of students gradually increased in number.
The Ruler of Jiangnan, Lady Li,
having heard of his reputation, invited him to the capital and appointed him to preside over the Great Monastery of Qingliang.
The state honored him with ever-increasing reverence,
and followers from all quarters flocked to him in ever-greater numbers;
even until now, his teachings are spread throughout the world.
